reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / Low's Clinical Autonomic Disorders
clinicalPearls: Presents with labile, volatile blood pressure, with episodic severe hypertension alternating with hypotension, reflecting loss of buffering of blood-pressure fluctuations
Hypertensive surges are often accompanied by tachycardia, headache, flushing, sweating, and emotional distress
Commonly follows neck surgery or radiotherapy for head and neck cancer, bilateral carotid body tumour resection, or damage to the glossopharyngeal and vagal afferents
May mimic phaeochromocytoma because of paroxysmal hypertension with catecholamine surges
A later chronic phase can show orthostatic tachycardia and pressure lability rather than sustained hypertension
A reduced parasympathetic component can produce marked tachycardia, and the volatile swings make treatment difficult
Diagnosis is supported by demonstrating impaired baroreflex sensitivity on autonomic testing
Management focuses on damping the swings and avoiding emotional and physical triggers, with specialist input
reference.pathophysiology: The arterial baroreflex normally buffers moment-to-moment changes in blood pressure: baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense arterial stretch and, via glossopharyngeal and vagal afferents to the brainstem, adjust sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow to keep pressure stable. Baroreflex failure occurs when these afferent limbs or their central connections are damaged, for example by surgery, radiotherapy, tumour, or neck trauma, so that blood pressure is no longer buffered. Sympathetic outflow becomes unrestrained and highly sensitive to arousal and stress, producing large surges of hypertension and tachycardia interspersed with hypotension when sympathetic drive falls. Loss of vagal baroreflex control adds heart-rate instability.
additionalDifferentials: Essential or secondary hypertension with anxiety
additionalInvestigations: Continuous or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring to document lability
Baroreflex sensitivity testing during formal autonomic assessment
Plasma and urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma
Imaging of the neck to identify prior surgery, radiotherapy, or tumour-related damage
Cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests including the Valsalva manoeuvre and deep breathing
redFlags: Severe hypertensive surges risking stroke or cardiac events
Symptoms strongly suggesting phaeochromocytoma requiring exclusion
Profound hypotensive episodes causing syncope and injury
A new neurological deficit occurring during a surge
reference.prognosis: Blood-pressure lability may lessen over time as partial compensation develops, but many patients have persistent, difficult-to-control fluctuations; prognosis depends on the extent of afferent damage and on avoiding hypertensive complications.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the paroxysmal hypertension as phaeochromocytoma and missing the true cause
Treating the hypertension aggressively and precipitating dangerous hypotension
Overlooking a history of neck surgery or radiotherapy
Underestimating the role of emotional and physical arousal as triggers
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Central sympatholytic agents such as clonidine to blunt hypertensive surges and sympathetic overactivity
Benzodiazepines to reduce arousal- and stress-triggered pressure surges
Short-acting vasodilators for acute hypertensive crises, with cautious pressor or fluid support during hypotensive episodes
Avoidance of physical and emotional triggers that provoke sympathetic surges
Management of the reduced parasympathetic component, including cardiac pacing where profound bradycardia or heart-rate instability occurs
Continuous or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring to guide titration of therapy
Referral to an autonomic specialist centre for baroreflex assessment and individualised management
